content: 1. Establish a clear procedure for referring specimens or individuals for additional testing to confirm their HIV status. This ensures accurate diagnosis and appropriate follow-up care. 2. Develop a policy detailing actions to take and documentation requirements when errors or adverse events occur during or after testing. Examples include invalid test results, failed quality control (QC), suspected false HIV-positive or HIV-negative results, or adverse client reactions when reporting HIV status. 3. Create a specific policy for managing false HIV-positive test results. This is critical as it may indicate issues with the testing system, including operator error. 4. Implement a policy on the use of protective equipment and proper disposal of sharps and biological waste to ensure safety and compliance with health standards. 5. If applicable, establish procedures for referring clients to additional services such as linkage to care, partner services, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), behavioral interventions, or other necessary services like housing, STI treatment, mental health support, or substance use programs. 6. Organize testing services to align with the needs of the community, ensuring high-quality service and accessibility. This may involve adjusting operating hours, minimizing client wait times, and fostering a stigma-free and discrimination-free environment. 7. Quality assurance should be an ongoing responsibility shared by all staff members, not a one-time activity or the sole responsibility of a single individual. 8. Ensure that policies, processes, and procedures are tailored to the assay formats used, the available infrastructure, and the skills of the staff. 9. Designate a staff member as the quality assurance focal point to oversee all aspects of the testing site’s operations. 10. Commit to professional quality standards in HIV testing, with regular management reviews of quality data, including turnaround times, invalid result rates, QC, and external quality assessment (EQA) data. 11. Develop an organizational chart that clearly defines the roles and responsibilities of all personnel involved in the testing process. 12. Employ sufficient trained and proficient personnel to handle all phases of the testing process, including pre-analytical (specimen collection and processing), analytical (assay procedures and result recording), and post-analytical (result interpretation and reporting). 13. Define the roles and responsibilities of all personnel, including who collects specimens, performs testing, conducts QC, issues reports, double-checks results, and handles data entry and cleaning tasks. 14. Ensure all personnel are adequately qualified and demonstrate proficiency in their assigned tasks. Provide both pre-service and in-service training on HIV testing. 15. Emphasize the importance of continuing education, particularly for sites with low client throughput or infrequent testing schedules. Regular supportive supervision and ongoing mentoring are essential. 16. Maintain training checklists for all staff to document their ongoing proficiency and encourage annual performance appraisals to address any issues affecting task performance. 17. Ensure that testing sites have appropriate and fully functional equipment, whether using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) or laboratory-based in vitro diagnostics (IVDs). This includes timing devices, refrigerators for temperature-sensitive materials, and calibrated equipment for accurate results. 18. Monitor storage and testing areas with thermometers, maintain an inventory of all equipment, and ensure preventive and corrective maintenance is performed as needed. Clearly label and remove non-functional equipment from service. 19. Develop standard operating procedures (SOPs) for all equipment, including instructions for operation, cleaning, and maintenance. 20. Prevent stock-outs of HIV test kits and essential consumables like gloves, lancets, alcohol swabs, specimen transfer devices, and waste disposal containers. Stock-outs can compromise quality and client satisfaction. 21. Avoid splitting larger test kits into smaller quantities or interchanging components between kits, as this can lead to errors and inaccurate results. 22. Implement robust quality control (QC) processes to ensure testing procedures are performed correctly, environmental conditions are suitable, and assays function as expected. QC should detect, evaluate, and correct errors before test results are reported. 23. Use internal QC processes within assays, such as control lines/spots in RDTs, to verify proper procedure functionality. Supplement with external QC materials validated by experienced providers. 24. Run external QC specimens weekly, for new operators, with new test kit lots or shipments, and when environmental conditions deviate from manufacturer recommendations. 25. If external QC results are unexpected, consider all test results since the last correct QC run invalid and retest individuals tested during this period. 26. Establish criteria for specimen acceptance or rejection, storage, retention, disposal, and referral to other sites for testing. 27. Ensure a second trained reader performs a blinded interpretation of visually read assays to confirm results. Discrepancies between readers should be resolved by a third reader. 28. Implement information management systems, whether paper-based or electronic, to record, store, and retrieve testing information securely. Assign unique patient identifiers to minimize errors and protect confidentiality. 29. Maintain accurate documentation to ensure HIV status reports are delivered to the correct individuals and can be traced if needed. Documentation should include policy records, procedural records, QC/EQA results, maintenance logs, and inventory records. 30. Establish occurrence management processes to detect and document non-conformances, identify root causes, and implement corrective and preventive actions. Examples include higher-than-expected rates of discrepant test results or deviations from documented procedures.
